**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 1:**

(p-335) Surat al-Inshiqaq

Its purpose is to demonstrate what was mentioned at the end of al-Mutaffifin: that the friends of God are granted bliss and the enemies are punished, because they did not affirm the Resurrection or the being presented before the King who brought them into existence and nurtured them, just as kings present their slaves and judge between them, and thus they are divided into the people of reward and the people of punishment. Its name, al-Inshiqaq (the Splitting), is the strongest indication of this, through reflection on the adverbial clause (zarf) and its response (jawab), which points to the discerning critic, and its reckoning. (In the name of God) Possessor of majesty and honor, (the Most Merciful) whose blessing is perfect, encompassing the special and the general, (the Especially Merciful) who completed it after generality upon His friends, thus making them happy by completing the favor.

* *

When it concluded al-Mutaffifin with the statement that the friends of God are in bliss and the enemies are in hellfire, as reward and punishment, it began this surah by swearing an oath to that effect, saying: ﴿When the sky splits open﴾, meaning, by what it possesses of firm construction, greatness and wisdom, which none other than Him, may His power be exalted, can match, ﴿splits open﴾, meaning it becomes weak and opens doorways, so it is ruined and collapses. This is after rising from the graves, as has passed in al-Haqqah concerning one of the two narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.

**Ṭabaʿī**, no—this is al-Biqāʿī's *Nazm al-Durar*. Translation follows.

"And it hearkens" (*wa-adhinat*), meaning it is exceedingly receptive, obedient, and submissive, in the most complete manner, like one who has an attentive ear and a soul at rest and well-pleased. ﴿To its Lord﴾, meaning to the command of the One who originated it and who manages all of its affairs. Although it is now submissive, its submission is apparent to most of creation, and they are the ones who affirm (*al-muthabbitah*). As for the deniers (*al-muʿaṭṭilah*), they sometimes attribute its effects to natures and stars. But at the splitting asunder (*inshiqaq*), complete disclosure occurs, so no one has any doubt left. ﴿And it is worthy﴾, in the passive form, meaning that it is innately disposed to recognize that this is a right (*haqq*) incumbent upon it and established for it; it is thus deserving of it, because it is a creature nourished by Him, glory be to Him, and every creature nourished is deserving of submission to its Lord. It has never ceased to be obedient to Him in its beginning and its end; but there, complete disclosure will be made to all of mankind.

When He began with the upper world, because it is more noble, being higher in rank and place, He followed with the lower world, saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the earth﴾, that is, [upon] what it has of solidity, thickness and density. By using the passive form, He indicated the ease with which the act is done to it by Him, glorified and exalted is He, and the swiftness of its response, even though it is more remarkable than the splitting of the sky, for a thing may be weakened by the long passage of time upon it, unlike the case of the earth. So He said: ﴿is stretched out﴾, that is, it is spread out like a hide, and stretched and extended, so that its extent is greatly increased after it was levelled, becoming flat, so its mountains, hills and mounds disappear, and you see in it no crookedness or unevenness, just as a hide, when it is stretched, becomes like that: its folds vanish and it expands.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 4:

(p-337) Since the skin is apt, when it is stretched, to reveal everything that is within it other than itself, He said: ﴿And it casts out what is in it﴾, meaning it expels what is in its belly of treasures, wealth and the dead, expelling it swiftly, as if it hurls it forth with a throw, and this too is like a carpet when it is shaken out. ﴿And it empties itself﴾, meaning it deliberately and laboriously strives to be empty of that and to relinquish it with the utmost of its effort, that is, He, glorified is He, did that act [as an act in which the earth was as if it were itself the doer of it in this manner, so that it became empty of everything that had been in its belly, and what was in its belly came forth onto its surface,

Since this might have led someone to think that it happens without His command, He, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿And it has listened to its Lord﴾, meaning that it did this by the permission of the Creator and Nurturer [of it], and it was affected in this by His influence, not by itself. It did all of this as the one who hears and responds does. ﴿And is worthy﴾, meaning that it was fit for this, just as every created thing is in this state. The repetition of "when" (idhā) serves to draw attention to the great power contained in each of the two clauses. The answer [to the conditional] is omitted, because it is entirely clear from what the context indicates, together with what preceded in al-Mutaffifin and the surahs before it, and what comes later in this surah. Its estimated meaning is: Everyone will certainly be called to account for all of his exertion, so the disbelievers will certainly be repaid for what they used to do, and the people of Islam will certainly be recompensed for what they used to do.

Abu Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: Because the previous surah (al-Infitar) introduced the recording angels (al-hafazah) and their enumeration of the servants' deeds in their books, the discussion returned to mentioning what is recorded for the righteous and the wicked, and the settling of that in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyun﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 7]. He followed this with a description of the taking of these books on the Day of Resurrection at the time of the presentation, and that taking them in the right hand is a sign of happiness, while taking them behind the back is a sign of wretchedness. This is because, in the two surahs before the mention of the books, it had been stated that they settle according to the differences in their contents: some of them are in ʿIlliyyun and some are in Sijjin until the Day of Presentation. Then each one is given his book, so one who takes it in his right hand, which is a sign of his happiness, and one who takes it from behind his back, which is a sign of his ruin. Thus the report about these books was completed: their origin, their settling, and their separation on the Day of Presentation. The surah opened with mention of the splitting of the sky, the spreading out of the earth, its casting forth of what is in it, and its being adorned, as an introduction to this great day, by which whoever has been preceded by happiness is reminded. The connection (munasabah) is clear. End.

Since the answer is what I have mentioned, he follows it with its explanation, saying, calling out with a particle suitable for distance (because the one being called is far from the one calling, and the one calling is the nearest of the ranks), beginning with the allies (al-awliya'), because the end of the defrauding (al-tatfif), of which this is the explanation, is bringing joy to them: ﴿O humankind [i.e. - ] who are familiar with his own self, forgetful of his Lord.﴾ And since most people deny the resurrection (al-ba'th), he emphasized, saying: ﴿Indeed you are toiling (kadih)﴾, i.e., striving and laboring with exertion for your own self, for good (khayr) or evil (shar) (p-339), and most of it is what leaves scratches, blemish, corruption and dispersion, ending ﴿at your Lord﴾, who brought you into existence and nurtured you, through working by what He wills in meaning, and through death in the sensory sense. He pointed to the striving of each person in what he is engaged in, and he made it an emphatic object with the verbal noun, saying: ﴿toiling﴾, i.e., great, ﴿so you will meet Him﴾, i.e., so your toil will be followed by your meeting with your Lord, and it will become manifest to you that in your journey toward Him you were like one striving in his meeting with exertion of one who competes with another in that. All of this is a figurative expression of the enforcement of His will and the execution of His decrees by means of arriving at Him. Its reality is that you will encounter His recompense, and there will be revealed to you from the greatness of His matter [what - ] that is revealed to the one who meets with the one he meets because of the meeting. This is a matter in which you strive to the utmost extent, because whoever has night and day as his two mounts, they surely bring him, whether he wills or not, to the end of his journey. So mentioning this in this manner is an exhortation to striving for excellence in action, because whoever is certain that he must be presented before the King exhausts his effort in working by what will earn his praise at the time of meeting Him.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 7:

Since it is well known that when a king's servants are presented before him, some of them are accepted and some rejected, because their striving is sometimes good and sometimes bad, [God] said, making known that the matter at His meeting is likewise [as we are accustomed to see]. Whoever is accepted is given the book of his good deeds in his right hand, because in the world he was among the people of the right, that is, the pleasing religion. Whoever is rejected is given his book in his left hand, because in the world he was with the people of the left, which is the false religion, acting without the permission of the Owner, as though he were doing so behind His back. He expressed this purpose with His words, glorified and exalted be He, explaining for mankind, which is meant as a collective noun, gathering the pronoun after having used the singular to specify the gathering of each individual: ﴿As for him who is given﴾. He made the verb passive to indicate that all matters of the Hereafter are subjugation and utterly easy for Him, glorified and exalted be He. In this world, the matter is for the command, and although it is so, the difference lies in the unveiling of the veil of causes there, so no one has any claim. ﴿His book﴾, that is, the record of his reckoning, which the angels wrote while he neither knows nor perceives it. ﴿In his right hand﴾, from in front of him, and he is the believer who obeys.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 8:

﴿So he will be called to a reckoning﴾ meaning: his reckoning will take place by a promise that admits no breaking, even if the term is long, to manifest majesty, greatness, and dominance. ﴿An easy reckoning﴾ meaning: an easy one, in which he is not scrutinized, because he used to call his own self to account, so that transgression came to him only through heedlessness. For this reason his deeds are presented, and He accepts their good and pardons their evil.

(p. 341) When this indicated forgiveness, he followed it with what indicates honour, saying: ﴿And he will return﴾, meaning he returns of his own accord, without being driven, with desire and acceptance, ﴿to his people﴾, meaning those whom God made his family (ahl) in Paradise. So he will know them better, and will know his station there better, than he knew his station in this world. Since happiness consists in the presence of joy without any constraint, he used the passive form in his words ﴿joyful﴾ [meaning] he has been given a Garden and silk. In this world, he was among his family anxious about the Reckoning before God, distressed and troubled, calling himself to account morning and evening with a severe reckoning, together with the hardship of his family, the narrowness of his livelihood, and the harm done by those who opposed him. So here he mentioned the fruit and the cause, because it is the intended end in itself. In the other half [of the comparison] he mentioned the means and the root.

The truthful one, Ummul-Mu'minin ʿĀʾisha (may God be pleased with her), found this verse problematic in light of what was narrated from her in the Sahih (the authentic collection) in two wordings. One of them is: "No one is reckoned with but he is destroyed," and the second is: "Whoever is scrutinized in reckoning is punished." ʿĀʾisha (may God be pleased with her) said: "I said: O Messenger of God! Does God not say: ﴿As for him who is given his record﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 7], to the end of the verse?" He (ﷺ) said: "That is only the presentation (ʿarḍ)."

If the first wording is the one she heard, the problem is clear, because it reduces to a universal affirmative proposition (kulliyya mujiba), namely "everyone who is reckoned with is destroyed," while the verse reduces to a particular negative proposition (juziyya salba), namely "some of those who are reckoned with are not destroyed." These are contradictory (naqid). In that case the second wording would be a transmission alteration by the narrators. If the second wording is the one she heard, the way to resolve the problem is to say: scrutiny (munaqasha) in language means exhaustive investigation, which is reaching the ultimate limit, and in reckoning this consists in mentioning the great and the small and recompensing for them. So the matter again reduces to a universal affirmative proposition, namely "everyone reckoned with respect to all his deeds is punished," and this includes every reckoning, whether easy or not, since the general includes all its particulars. The verse, however, affirms that whoever is given his record in his right hand is reckoned with but is not destroyed. ʿĀʾisha (may God be pleased with her) knew that the record contains all deeds, from God's words: ﴿It leaves out no small thing nor great thing but has counted it﴾ [al-Kahf: 49], and from the hadith about the two recording angels (al-ḥafiẓīn), and other things. So the matter returns to this: some of those who are reckoned with respect to all their deeds are not destroyed. In that case there appears to be a contradiction, so she asked, and he (ﷺ) confirmed the difficulty for her and answered her with what amounts to this: the meaning of "reckoning" in the hadith is its literal denotation (mutabaqa), which is mentioning all the deeds and receiving recompense for each of them, and this is the meaning of scrutiny. So the meaning of "whoever is scrutinized in reckoning" is whoever is reckoned with a real reckoning, by mentioning all his deeds and receiving recompense for each one. The meaning of "reckoning" in the verse is a part of the literal meaning, namely the mentioning of deeds alone without recompense. This is by implicative denotation (tadammun), as a metaphorical usage by way of a related meaning (majaz mursal), since it applies the name of the whole to a part. For this reason, ʿĀʾisha (may God be pleased with her) afterwards said, explaining the verse: "He is made to acknowledge his sins, and then He overlooks them," as Abu Hayyan transmitted from her. This is also indicated by the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in what the two Shaykhs (al-Shaykhan, Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn ʿUmar (may God be pleased with them both): (p. 343) "God, may He be exalted, will bring the believer near on the Day of Resurrection, place His screen (kanaf) over him and cover him, then say to him: 'Do you know the sin of such-and-such?' until He makes him recall all his sins, and he sees in himself that he is ruined. The Lord, glorified is He, says: 'I concealed them for you in the world, and I forgive them for you today.'"

The word "kanaf" indicates this, for the kanaf of a bird is its wing, and when its chick is under its wing, it treats it with the utmost gentleness. God, the Most High, is more merciful and more gentle.

﴿As for him who is given his record﴾, meaning with the utmost ease, even if he himself would refuse that, ﴿his record﴾, meaning the scroll of his account, ﴿behind his back﴾, meaning in his left hand. The giving encompasses the whole direction of "behind," which is [عِلْمُ - ] the evil, because he used to do what God had not permitted. It is as if he acted from behind Him, supposing that it would be hidden from Him, the Glorified. So he deserves that his right hand be chained to his neck, that his left hand be behind his back, and that his record be placed in it. This is an *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which two complementary elements are each left implicit, the mention of one indicating the other). The mention of the right hand first indicates the left [ثانِيًا- ], and the mention of "behind" second indicates "in front" [أوَّلًا]. The secret of this is that He mentioned the evidence of affection and gentleness, such as handshaking and the like, for the fortunate one, and the evidence of treachery and assassination for the wretched one.

﴿So he will call out for destruction﴾, i.e., with a promise that will certainly come to pass without doubt, ever. "Destruction" (thubūr) means grief and remorse, like his saying "Woe to me, O destruction!" (wa-thubūrāh). It is the ruin that encompasses every kind of hardship, because his deeds in the world were the deeds of those who are doomed.

(p-344) Since that (the perdition described) would not happen except through a great trial, he followed it with what could be its cause, saying: ﴿And he shall burn in a blazing Fire﴾. That is, he will be plunged into the Fire, which is at its most intense blazing, and will endure its heat. The verse is coordinated with the preceding one (ʿaṭf) and encompasses it, because he used to follow his desires, which surround the Fire, so they brought him to it and enveloped him.

When he mentioned this torment, which cannot be borne, he followed it with its cause, as a warning against it and an appeal toward repentance, and as a caution against joy in the abode of grief. So he said, emphasizing, to draw attention to the fact that it should not be believed that a person of intellect would have joy in this world: ﴿Indeed, he was﴾, meaning, by that which is for him like a natural disposition and temperament, ﴿among his people﴾, meaning in the abode of action, ﴿joyful﴾, meaning having joy firmly established for him, exulting in wealth and rank, rejoicing in it, relying on it, indulgent, given to luxury, with idleness and heedlessness regarding the remembrance of the reckoning of the Hereafter, as He said in the verse before it: ﴿And when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 31]. None of them grieves over a sin he has committed or a foul deed he has perpetrated; rather, he rejoices at having such things come to him. So he will be reckoned in the Hereafter with a severe reckoning, and he will return to his companions grieved and broken. It has become clear that the discourse contains ihtibak (elliptical balancing): the mention of the easy reckoning, which is the result and the effect, first indicates the omission of its opposite second, and the mention of joy among his people, which is the cause, in the second part indicates the omission of its opposite, which is the cause of happiness, namely grief, and the reckoning of the self in the first. So it is ihtibak within ihtibak. Then he gave the reason for the constancy of his joy, saying, emphasizing, also as a warning that it is not to be believed that anyone denies the Resurrection in light of the proofs he has, which are too numerous to be counted:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 14:

﴿Indeed, he thought﴾ because of the weakness of his insight, ﴿that﴾ i.e., that ﴿he would never return﴾, i.e., would go back to his Lord, or would be diminished, or would perish. ﴿And they say, "There is nothing but our worldly life; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time."﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24]. Therefore he used to act like one who does not fear the outcome

Yes indeed (﴿بَلى﴾), he will certainly return (to his Lord) diminished, reduced and ruined. Then he gave the reason for that, with His saying, emphasizing it for the sake of the one who denies it: ﴿Indeed, his Lord﴾, that is, the One who originated his creation and nurtured him, ﴿was﴾ eternally and everlastingly ﴿Seeing of him﴾, that is, of this wretched one, in his return just as He was in his origination, and in ﴿all his deeds and states, which it is not permissible for a just and equitable Judge to leave without reckoning﴾ for them. ﴿Seeing﴾, that is, watching over him and knowing him with the most penetrating watching and the most perfect knowledge. So for Him to leave him neglected, while knowing his deeds, would contradict wisdom, justice and sovereignty; it is something that is impossible for the intellect in any respect.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 16:

When Allah, glorified is He, reported their denial of what the messengers brought them concerning the Resurrection, in a manner that made clear the proof against the baselessness of their denial, and they did not turn back, He made the oath on the truth of that a consequence of it. This is because, for the warning, sincere and compassionate giver of counsel, after the establishment of proofs, nothing remains except to affirm by oath the truth of what he has said, out of his concern for the one being counselled and his compassion for him. Leaving off swearing about what is already evident is more eloquent than swearing, because such leaving off alerts the addressee to reflection and contemplation. So He said: ﴿So I swear﴾, meaning: I swear a great oath, one that is like the depths of the sea, by these matters which I will mention, because of what they indicate of the power to originate and to restore. I do not swear by them, though they are of the utmost greatness, because of their clear indications, since the thing sworn to is more august than them and more manifest, so it is independent of being sworn by. ﴿By the twilight﴾, meaning the light that appears in the west immediately after sunset, in layers: first red, then yellow, then murky, then to whiteness, then to blackness. Likewise the night, at its beginning, is white with a dusky tinge, and then its dusky tinge gradually increases until it becomes wholly black, and so it darkens everything. It is called shafaq (twilight redness) because of its thinness (riqqah), and from the same root comes shafaqah (compassion), because of the tenderness (riqqat) of the heart.

﴿By the night﴾, meaning the night that overcomes the day, covers it and drives it away, ﴿and what it gathers﴾, meaning that it gathers within its belly and drives and herds from that twilight (al-shafaq), from the day that came before it, from the stars that it brings forth, and from other wonders which indicate that their Originator brought them into being after they had not existed. The One who is able to do that is able to originate and to restore, and to do whatever He wills.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 18:

﴿And by the moon﴾, i.e., the one which is His sign, ﴿when it becomes full﴾, i.e., it is arranged, levels out, and its completeness is gathered together, and its matter is perfected on the night of its fullness (ibdar), after it had been absent entirely; then it began as a crescent (hilal), faint, slight, and thin, and it never ceased to increase until it became complete, then it diminishes until it disappears (p-347) then it returns to its state, a sign more manifest than the sun for the power of its Creator, likewise over every matter of origination and return.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 84, verse 19:

Since these matters are very great, none can accomplish them except Allah, the Exalted, and they have benefits which none knows in their true extent except He, glorified and exalted is He. Each of them, moreover, points to the complete power of Allah, exalted is He, over what is meant to be established and made clear to the intellects, namely the perfect power to restore a thing exactly as it was. The negation of swearing by them indicates that this matter is in the utmost clarity, so the matter does not need an oath. He said, at the place of the answer to the oath, joined with the lam that indicates the oath, mentioning what is so evident and self-evident that it needs no alerting to it by other than itself, He mentioned it: ﴿You will surely ride﴾, that is, O you who are responsible. This is according to the reading of the majority, with a damma on the ba', indicating the deletion of the waw of the plural. Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on it, on the basis that the address is to the human being in terms of the wording. ﴿Stage upon stage﴾ going beyond ﴿from stage to stage﴾, that is, state after state, from the phases of life and the stages of living and the agonies of death, then from the affairs of the barzakh (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection) and the circumstances of resurrection and the calamities of the gathering, as is shown by what was for you before that, equal by that power which brought those beings into existence and produced those wonders, equally. So you will be in a state of establishment of existence in (p-348) every stage, in the condition of being firmly upon a thing by riding. Each state is in agreement with the other in this, for a ṭabaq (layer, stage) is that which corresponds to another. From this it was said of a covering: ṭabaq, because of its correspondence to what it covers. A ṭabaq is anything that equals something else; it also refers to the surface of the earth, or a generation of time, or twenty years. All of these meanings are clear in what is intended here, and their being is self-evident. The first of the human stages is the embryo, then the newborn, then the suckling, then the weaned child, then the youth, then the man, then the young man, then the elder, then the old man, then the dead. After this comes the raising up, then the gathering, then the reckoning, then the weighing, then the Sirat, then the abode. Like these perceptible stages, there are also immaterial stages of virtues and vices.

When the purpose had become clear and nothing remained but obstinacy, the censure, rebuke, reproach and warning followed as a consequence. Turning away from addressing them to the third person, to indicate that they deserve to be seized if they do not return, He said: ﴿So what is wrong with them﴾, meaning: what is the matter with those to whom We sent down this Book, which is itself a miracle, that ﴿they do not believe﴾? That is, they do not bring faith into being and renew it at every moment, continually, in accordance with everything this Book calls to, the Book with which the King of kings singled them out. The proof has become manifest and the evidences have been established, especially the proofs of the Resurrection. Is it not merely one of these states through which they pass? For whoever is in one condition today and in another tomorrow is deserving of knowing that his management belongs to another. Whoever does not know this has no cure for his madness. Whoever knows that his management belongs to another, knowing that the will in management belongs to Him and not to himself, [ ... ]

It was said to Abu Bakr al-Warraq: "What is the proof of the Maker (al-Sani')?" He said: "The transformation of states, the weakness of power, the frailty of the pillars, the subjugation of will, and the dissolution of resolve."

﴿And when the Qur'an is recited to them﴾, that is, by whichever reciter it may be, ﴿the Qur'an﴾, that is, the one that gathers everything that benefits them in their worldly life and their hereafter, and that distinguishes between every ambiguous matter concerning the lawful and the unlawful and other things, ﴿they do not prostrate﴾, that is, they do not submit inwardly and humble themselves before the truth by prostration in the linguistic sense (al-sujud al-lughawi, prostration as humbling oneself), so that they perform with the body the legal prostration (al-sujud al-shar'i) upon its recitation. This is because it possesses speech that has made clear knowledge that cannot be exhausted, together with its testimony to itself, through its inimitability (i'jaz), that it is from Allah. They have no excuse in this except ignorance or incapacity, yet there is no ignorance in the presence of the Qur'an, nor incapacity where there is strength and free choice.

When this was a rhetorical question of denial (istifham inkari), whose meaning is negation, the implied sense was: "They do [not] believe, and they have no excuse for that at all." He turned away from that sense with the words ﴿Rather﴾, and he placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to generalize and to draw attention to the attribute that led them to denial. So he said ﴿those who disbelieve﴾, meaning those who concealed the mirrors of their intellects that point to the truth, ﴿deny﴾, meaning the Qur'an and what it indicates of the lofty realities of gnosis (al-irfan) that raise one to the peak of faith in the One, the Judge (al-Dayyan). (p-٣٥٠)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 23:

﴿And Allah﴾, that is, while the state is that the King, who encompasses everything in power and knowledge, ﴿is most knowing﴾, that is, of them, of themselves, ﴿of what they conceal﴾, that is, what they place in the receptacles of their breasts of disbelief and enmity, owing to the desires that occupy them, namely the love of leadership and the claim to divinity, which occupy them away from pondering this Qur'an and away from the evidences found in existing things.

Since this warrants severe warning, he placed in its position, in mockery of them and to inform that the wrath has reached its furthest extent, his saying: ﴿So give them tidings﴾, meaning: inform them, O best of creation, most complete and most just in report, of a report that changes their joy, ﴿of a painful punishment﴾, meaning: of intense pain, because of the severity of its afflicting. If there was ever a day for them of good tidings, then this is it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 84, verse 25:

When He had informed of their humiliation, and had expressed them by the lowest of the teeth (i.e., the lowest of the eaters of stripped flesh) as an indication that among them are those who accept faith, He made an exception of them, saying: ﴿Except those who have believed﴾, meaning they acknowledged faith, ﴿and done righteous deeds﴾, as an indication of the sincerity of their faith, ﴿the good deeds﴾.

Since it has preceded that whoever is brought to account is punished, and that the one who is saved will have his reckoning made light, he (al-Biqa'i) knew that deeds have no real bearing on the reward. The basis is, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, on being covered by mercy, to the extent that even the bliss is called a reward. He dropped the fa' (the particle indicating causation, "so") to draw attention to this, unlike what is in Surat al-Tin, because of what comes later about its context requiring the fa'. So He said: ﴿For them is a reward﴾, meaning a great reward and an abundant recompense known to Allah the Exalted, which is the overlooking of their minor sins and the concealing of them, ﴿unending﴾, meaning uncut or diminished, or [one] He does not bestow upon them with reproach, in this world and the Hereafter. They shall receive that on the Day of Religion, the Day when the sky is split open and the earth is stretched out, and the disbelievers return to what they used to do. Thus its last part has returned upon its first, and its joint has been firmly linked to its connector.
